summary: Registers the MIME sub-type audio/32KADPCM for toll quality audio at 32 kbit/s. This lets voice recordings in that format be labeled properly in email. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 3802.

eli5.summary: A label that tells email programs that an attachment is a particular kind of voice recording, so they know how to play it back.

questions: how is adpcm audio sent in mime
subtitle: A standardized MIME type for sending compressed voice audio in email.

tldr.problem: Voice recordings need a standard label when sent in email so receiving programs know they contain compressed audio and how to decode it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2422 registers the MIME media type audio/32KADPCM for voice audio encoded using the ITU-T G.726 standard at 32 kbit/s (ADPCM compression).
tldr.outcome: Email and voice messaging systems can reliably exchange compressed voice data with a clear, standardized content type. RFC 3802 superseded this specification.

today: RFC 2422 is a Proposed Standard that was superseded by RFC 3802. The audio/32KADPCM MIME type registration remains in use in voice messaging and VPIM implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2422 registers a MIME media subtype for compressed voice audio. The registration standardizes how email and messaging systems label and handle voice data encoded in 32 kbit/s ADPCM format, based on the ITU-T Recommendation G.726.

This MIME type is central to the Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM), a specification for sending voice messages and voice documents over email.
sections.eli5: This document says 'here is the official way to label a voice message so email programs understand it.'

sections.title: The G.726 Encoding
sections.content:
ITU-T Recommendation G.726 defines Adaptive Differential Pulse Code Modulation (ADPCM), a technique for compressing voice audio. It converts a standard 64 kbit/s telephone signal (A-law or u-law PCM, sampled at 8000 times per second) down to 32, 24, or 16 kbit/s.

The 32 kbit/s rate—the subject of this RFC—preserves toll quality voice, meaning it sounds like a telephone call. The algorithm adapts to the signal as it processes, which is why it's called 'adaptive.' It replaced the earlier ITU-T G.721 standard, which only specified 32 kbit/s ADPCM.
sections.eli5: G.726 takes a phone call and squeezes it down to use less data. At 32 kbit/s it still sounds like a phone call, not like a robot.

sections.title: MIME Media Type Definition
sections.content:
RFC 2422 defines the MIME media type audio/32KADPCM to hold binary voice data encoded exactly as specified by G.726. The audio stream has no header; it is pure encoded audio data.

The content transfer encoding is typically binary or base64 depending on the mail system's capabilities. No MIME parameters are required; all audio data is assumed to be G.726 encoded at 32 kbit/s.

Applications using this type (such as voice messaging) may add descriptive headers such as Content-Description and Content-Disposition to label the audio in human-readable terms, but these are not part of the media type definition itself.
sections.eli5: The MIME type is just a label: audio/32KADPCM. It tells the email program 'this is voice audio compressed in a specific way, with no header info.'

sections.title: Byte Ordering
sections.content:
G.726 encodes audio as 4-bit code words. When packing pairs of these into bytes, little endian ordering is used: the first code word (A) goes into the four least significant bits of the byte, and the second code word (B) goes into the four most significant bits.

Within each code word, the least significant bit of A is in bit 0 (rightmost) and its most significant bit is in bit 3. Similarly, bits 4–7 hold B, with B's least significant bit in bit 4 and most significant bit in bit 7.

This ordering is defined in ITU-T Recommendation X.420 (the X.400 email standard) and is the only ordering permitted for audio/32KADPCM. If voice samples have an odd number of code words, the last unpaired code word is discarded; padding with silence to an even count is preferred.
sections.eli5: The technical detail: two small 4-bit numbers fit in one byte. The RFC specifies exactly which 4 bits hold the first number and which hold the second, so all systems pack them the same way.

sections.title: Interoperability and Considerations
sections.content:
One interoperability issue is that some existing G.726 codecs use a different bit ordering (big endian instead of little endian). Implementations supporting the opposite ordering must reorder the code words when converting to or from audio/32KADPCM format.

From a security perspective, there are no known risks with sending or playing raw audio data. The audio codec interprets the data; any corrupted or unintended information in the bit stream results in noise, not in a security violation. The data is binary, so it must be encoded (usually in base64) to transit mail systems that do not support binary attachments.
sections.eli5: If you have an older voice system that packs bits differently, you have to convert. And audio data can't hurt you—bad data just sounds like static.
